title: This One jQuery Mistake Froze Our Web Page! Here's the Fix You Need to Know
author: Niaz Bin Siraj
excerpt: A real-world debugging story about how using .appendTo() inside a loop caused our web page to freeze, and how DocumentFragment saved the day.
contents:
It was a normal morning at the office. We were working on a feature that shows a list of items on a web page using jQuery. Everything looked fine - until one of my teammates Adyel Ullahil Mamun noticed the page was acting weird.

Whenever the number of items increased, the browser became slow, sometimes even unresponsive. At first, we thought it was a server issue or maybe too much data. But no - the problem was hiding inside a small line of jQuery.

Let me show you.

The Problematic Code

items.forEach(item => {
  $('<li></li>').text(item.name).appendTo('#item-list');
});

Looks simple, right? It just adds each item to a list. But here's the hidden danger...

The Problem with .appendTo() in a Loop

When you use .appendTo() inside a loop, jQuery updates the DOM again and again, for each item. That means:

  • Your browser does a lot of extra work.
  • On large data, this becomes super slow.
  • The page can freeze or crash.
warning
Why This Happens

Every call to .appendTo() triggers a DOM reflow - the browser has to recalculate layout, repaint, and update the render tree. Inside a loop with hundreds or thousands of items, this adds up fast.

What Happens Inside the Loop
Loop Iteration→.appendTo()→DOM Reflow→Repaint
This cycle repeats for every single item, causing N reflows for N items.

That's exactly what was happening to us.

The Smart Fix: Use DocumentFragment

My teammate, sharp-eyed and smart, suggested a better way.

Instead of adding each item to the page one by one, we should first build everything in memory using a documentFragment - and then add it once to the page.

Here's the refactored version:

const fragment = $(document.createDocumentFragment());

items.forEach(item => {
  $('<li></li>').text(item.name).appendTo(fragment);
});

$('#item-list').append(fragment);
lightbulb
Why This Works

A DocumentFragment is a lightweight, in-memory container that is not part of the live DOM. When you append elements to it, no reflows or repaints happen. Only when the entire fragment is appended to the actual DOM does a single reflow occur.

And just like that - the page was smooth again!

Before
N Reflows
Each .appendTo() in the loop triggers a separate DOM reflow and repaint cycle.
After
1 Reflow
DocumentFragment batches all changes into a single DOM update at the end.

Why DocumentFragment?

  • DocumentFragment lets you build your elements in memory, not directly on the page.
  • You avoid many DOM updates - only one final update happens.
  • Your page becomes faster, even with large data.
Key Rule
Batch Your DOM Updates

If you are using .appendTo() inside a loop, stop and think: Can I build everything first and append once? This single change can save your users from frustration and keep your page lightning fast.

Key Takeaways

  1. Avoid DOM manipulation inside loops. Each .appendTo() call inside a loop triggers a full reflow, which compounds rapidly with data size.
  2. Use DocumentFragment for batch inserts. Build your elements in memory first, then insert them all at once with a single DOM operation.
  3. Small code changes, big impact. It's amazing how a small mistake in a few lines of code can have a big impact. Thanks to my teammate's sharp eye, a quick refactor solved the freeze entirely.

So next time your page starts lagging, check your loops - .appendTo() might be the silent troublemaker!
